studies.title: The Complaint That Was Heard
studies.meaning: The surah opens by reporting that a conversation has already been overheard. A woman pressed her case about her husband and, not satisfied with the answer she was given, turned the matter upward. The ayah does not summarise her argument or name her. It records twice that the hearing happened, and then closes with two names, Hearing and Seeing, so the report of one exchange widens into a statement about every exchange. Only afterwards does the surah address the practice she was protesting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report with unusual agreement that a woman of Medina came about a spoken formula her husband had used, a pre-Islamic device that cut a wife off without releasing her. She was told that nothing had yet come down on the matter, and she kept pressing while praying aloud about it. The passage that follows was the answer, and the surah takes its name from her.

keyTerms.note: A verb of sustained back-and-forth, not a single request. The form implies two sides pressing a case. The Quran uses it of her without a syllable of criticism, which is what makes its placement striking.
From a root for opening up a difficulty before someone else. The form carries the sense of doing it for one's own relief, so the word covers unburdening as much as petitioning for a verdict.
A word for speech turned back and forth between two people. It makes the object of the divine hearing a dialogue, both halves of it, rather than only the appeal addressed upward.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage in Arabia was arranged between families, and a woman's standing in a dispute usually ran through her male relatives. If her own household had already settled the matter, she had no court to appeal to and nobody obliged to argue for her. Speaking her own case, at length, to the man leading the community was outside the ordinary shape of things. Anyone watching would have registered how far outside it was.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only surah of the Quran in which the name God appears in every single ayah, all twenty-two of them. It is also named for a woman rather than for a prophet, a people or a natural sign, and the Arabic title is a participle: the woman who argues her case.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hearing is established before any instruction is given, which sets the order of the whole surah: a private grievance is answered first, and the general provision is drawn out of it second. The two names at the close are load-bearing. Setting Hearing beside Seeing covers what is spoken and what is not, so a person with no standing before any human authority is not thereby outside the audience.

crossReferences.why: States the nearness this ayah demonstrates, promising an answer to the one who calls, with no intermediary named.
Jacob uses the same verb for laying out a grievance, and says he directs it to God alone.
Asks who answers the distressed person when he calls, framing it as something only God does.

studies.applyIt: Think of a complaint you have decided is too small to raise, or one you raised once and got no answer to. Say it out loud, in your own words, the next time you pray. Do not tidy it into something more presentable first. What this ayah records being heard was the untidied version, argued at length by someone nobody expected to argue.

studies.title: They Are Not Their Mothers
studies.meaning: The formula men used is quoted and then contradicted on factual grounds before anything else is said about it. A wife is not a mother, and motherhood is defined narrowly and physically: mothers are the women who gave birth. The saying is then given two labels, something the mind rejects and a distortion, which the commentators read as covering its moral wrongness and its untruth together. The ayah ends on pardon, so the correction and the way back arrive in the same sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the complaint the surah opens with. The practice belonged to pre-Islamic Arabia: a husband declared his wife like his mother's back and treated the marriage as suspended without dissolving it. She could not remarry and had no claim on him. The commentators name the woman's case as the occasion for these ayat, and describe this as the first passage to address the practice at all.

keyTerms.note: Built on the ordinary word for a back, from the phrase men actually used. It names an act of speech rather than a state of feeling, which is why the reply begins by testing whether the speech is true.

The word appears three times in this one ayah: denied, defined, then denied again by implication. Repetition does the arguing. The claim is dismantled by restating the term rather than by threatening anyone.
From a root meaning to lean away from something. It is the word standing behind false testimony elsewhere in the Quran, which files the formula under lying rather than under mere bad manners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kinship in Arabia was legal architecture rather than sentiment. Who counted as your mother settled inheritance, whom you could marry, who owed blood money on your behalf, and which men were obliged to defend you. A husband declaring his wife a mother was not speaking poetically. He was trying to shift her across a line the whole social order rested on, and the entire cost of the move landed on her.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this formula once more, at 33:4, where it is set beside two other fictions about kinship: that a man has two hearts inside him, and that an adopted son is a son by blood. All three are answered the same way, by pointing out that saying a thing does not make it so.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A speech act is denied the power to reshape reality. Words can bind a speaker and can wrong a listener, but they do not rewrite what a person is, and the ayah settles that before it discusses consequences. Pardon is then named immediately, which keeps the passage from reading as condemnation of the men involved. The wrong is described accurately and the door is left open in the same breath.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same formula alongside adoption, denying that any spoken claim can create a blood relationship.
Grounds all kinship in a single origin, which is the background this ayah's definition of motherhood assumes.
Treats careless speech about others as a serious matter rather than as words that pass harmlessly.

studies.applyIt: Notice a phrase you use about someone close to you when you are angry, the one that assigns them a category rather than describing what they did. Say the description instead the next time, even if it takes longer. This ayah spends its whole length separating what a person is from what was said about them, and it does that before it discusses any remedy.

studies.title: A Price Between Word And Return
studies.meaning: A remedy is attached to the formula rather than a punishment. Where a man used the saying and then goes back on it, the freeing of a person from bondage stands between the words and the resumption of the marriage. Commentators differ over what going back means: withdrawing the words, wanting the wife again, or repeating the formula. They agree the release comes first. The ayah calls the whole arrangement an admonition rather than a fine, and closes on God's awareness of what is actually done.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah's opening episode continues: the husband had spoken the formula, then wanted the marriage on ordinary terms again, while his wife had spent the interval neither married nor free to remarry. Nothing in the customs of Arabia dissolved the saying or ended the suspension. The commentators read these ayat as the answer to that specific impasse, framed so that it covers every later case.

keyTerms.note: The verb only says return, without saying return to what. That gap is where the classical readings divide, and the Quran leaves it open rather than defining the trigger it attaches the remedy to.
The word for the back of the neck, used across the Quran for a human being held in bondage. Freeing is expressed as loosening a neck, which keeps the physical fact of restraint inside the vocabulary.
A passive from a root for counsel that moves the heart, not for penalty. It files the whole provision under teaching, so the release is presented as instruction rather than as a price paid.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bondage was ordinary in Arabian households: captives from raids, people sold at market, debtors who had lost their standing. A freed person did not vanish; they usually stayed attached to the household as a client. Setting one free meant giving up labour and status in front of neighbours who would notice. Tying the resumption of a marriage to that particular cost put the man's private words in public view, and put a second person's freedom on the other side of them.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for freeing a person from bondage occurs three times in the Quran, and each time it answers a different failure: this passage, a broken oath at 5:89, and an accidental killing at 4:92. In every case a lighter alternative follows for someone without the means, so the provision never depends on being wealthy enough to comply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not undo the harm by declaring the words void and moving on. It attaches a cost, and the cost is another person's freedom rather than a payment to the wronged wife or to a treasury. Something said carelessly inside a marriage is answered by a change in someone else's life entirely. The closing name for God's awareness covers the inward part of the act, which no outside observer could confirm.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same release of a person from bondage as the answer to an accidental killing, with the same fallback of fasting.
Sets out graded atonement for a broken oath, showing the same pattern of a cost scaled to what a person has.
Names the freeing of a person from bondage as the first thing on the ascent that surah describes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you said in a temper that you have since walked back with an apology and nothing more. Add one action to it this week, something that costs you a little and that the other person did not ask for. This passage sets a real price between the words and the return, and the price is what makes the return believable.

studies.title: The Ladder Down To Everyone
studies.meaning: Two fallbacks descend from the first: two consecutive months of fasting, then feeding sixty people in need. The ladder is built on capacity, so no one is left without a route back. Then comes the reason, and it is not restitution. The whole arrangement exists so that faith in God and His messenger is affirmed in something done rather than said. The word for limits arrives last, marking these as boundaries set by God rather than terms negotiated between the parties.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the provision begun in the previous ayah. Medina in this period was not uniformly wealthy; many of the emigrants had arrived with nothing and were being housed by others. A requirement that only a man with property could meet would have applied to part of the community and not the rest. The descending alternatives address that directly, and the commentators note the order runs from what costs most to what costs least.

keyTerms.note: A dual adjective from a root for following on someone's heels. What it measures is unbroken succession rather than a total number of days, which is why the classical discussion turns on continuity rather than on arithmetic.

From a root for stillness, describing someone whom poverty has brought to a standstill. It is distinguished in the tradition from the word for one who asks, since this person may be too settled in want to appear at anyone's door.

The word for the edge of a piece of land or the blade of a sword, the line where one thing stops. Naming these provisions boundaries frames them as territory with edges rather than as a list of demands.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sixty meals was a visible quantity in a town where a household counted its dates and barley by the measure. Feeding that many meant buying at market, cooking in batches, and being seen doing it. Two unbroken months of fasting was harder still for a man who worked in the sun or travelled with caravans. Neither alternative could be done quietly, which mattered in a settlement where everyone knew whose marriage was in trouble.
studies.didYouKnow: Two consecutive months of fasting appears in exactly two places in the Quran: here, and at 4:92, where it answers an accidental killing. The phrase naming the limits of God occurs seven times, spread across passages on fasting, divorce, inheritance and this one, which is what ties otherwise unrelated subjects into a single vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The stated purpose is striking. The graded requirement is not there to compensate anyone; it exists so that belief becomes something a person enacts. That turns an internal commitment into an event with a date and a cost. And by scaling the requirement to means, the passage refuses to make sincerity a function of wealth: the poorest man reaches the same endpoint as the richest, along a longer road.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same phrase about God's limits, there marking the boundaries of the fast rather than of a marriage.
Grades atonement for a broken oath the same way, descending until it reaches something anyone can do.
States the principle underneath the descending ladder, that no soul is charged beyond its capacity.

studies.applyIt: Look at a commitment you have quietly dropped because the version you first pictured was beyond you. Name the smaller version you could actually keep, and start there this week. The ladder in this passage descends deliberately. It does not treat the lower rung as failure; it treats reaching the ground at all as the point.

studies.title: Standing Across The Line
studies.meaning: The verb for opposition comes from the root just used for limits, so the picture is of people placing themselves on the far side of a boundary, not merely disagreeing. What follows is stated as already accomplished: they have been thrown back, as earlier peoples were. Between the two halves sits a single sentence about clear signs having been sent down, which supplies the reason the outcome is not arbitrary. The closing word for the punishment names humiliation rather than pain.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the surah turns here from a domestic case to open hostility. The community had opponents inside Medina as well as outside it, some of whom kept up the outward forms while working against the arrangement. The commentators do not attach a single occasion to this ayah; they read it against the general situation after the migration, with the appeal to earlier peoples serving as the argument from precedent.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root for a boundary or an edge. The form describes taking up the position on the other side of a line, which makes the opposition territorial in image rather than a matter of argument.

A passive from a root for being flung down on the face, used of a rout. It reports the outcome as finished, and the classical readers take the past tense as certainty rather than as a date already passed.

From a root for lowness and contempt. The Quran distinguishes it from the word for painful, so what is promised here is loss of standing rather than sensation, matched to people whose aim was standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was held in public and lost in public. A man's word carried because his kin backed it and because no one had seen him humiliated. Defeat in a raid cost animals, but the lasting damage was the story told afterwards at other people's fires. A poem naming a chief's disgrace outlived the event by generations. Promising humiliation rather than pain named the loss that society actually feared.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated as opposing here shares its root with the word for God's limits used one ayah earlier. Placing them back to back sets up a single image across two ayat: boundaries are drawn, and then people are described by where they stand relative to them. The same verb returns at 58:20, and the same root once more at 58:22.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rejection is treated as having a shape that recurs, so the passage argues from history rather than from threat alone. The middle clause is doing the moral work: signs were made clear, which is what makes the outcome an answer rather than a display of power. And by specifying humiliation, the passage locates the reversal precisely where the opposition invested, in reputation and position, not in the body.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same verb for opposition later in this surah, placing such people among the lowest.
Makes the same argument from precedent, pointing to earlier peoples who were stronger and were not spared.
Pairs the sending down of clarifying signs with guidance, which is the middle clause of this ayah stated on its own.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time a disagreement stops being about the question and becomes about your position in the room. That shift is what this ayah's verb describes. When you catch it, say the other person's argument back to them in your own words before you answer. It is a small way of stepping off the line and back into the discussion.

studies.title: Counted And Forgotten
studies.meaning: Two verbs are set against each other in the middle of the ayah, and the whole point sits in the gap between them. One party has kept a running tally; the other has mislaid the same material. Forgetting is presented not as innocence but as the ordinary human condition, which is exactly why the record matters. The Day is described as informing rather than accusing: what happens is that people are told what they did, in detail they no longer hold.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the warning to those who set themselves against the community. The surah is working through things said in private: a formula spoken inside a marriage, and, in the ayat just ahead, whispered plotting. This ayah answers the assumption underneath both, that quiet words spoken long ago have simply gone. No specific occasion is reported for it; its placement is what carries the argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for counting with pebbles, the way a herdsman kept a tally of animals passing a gate. The word is arithmetical rather than judicial: it names an exact count, not yet a verdict.
The plain verb for forgetting, with no blame built into it. Placing it directly beside the counting makes the contrast one of memory rather than of honesty, which is harder to argue with.

An intensive form from a root that covers both seeing and testifying. It carries presence at the event and the ability to report it afterwards, which is why the same word serves for a witness in court.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Records in Medina were mostly memory. Debts were held in the heads of the parties and their witnesses, and a dispute a few years old came down to whose recollection the community trusted. Written contracts existed but were rare enough that the Quran had to instruct people to draw them up. In that world, an exact and permanent count of everything a person had done was not a familiar object at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The longest ayah in the Quran, 2:282, is the instruction to write down debts, and it runs to well over a hundred words about scribes, witnesses and dictation. Set beside it, this ayah describes a ledger that needs none of that apparatus, and the episode opening this same surah turned on a spoken formula nobody had written down.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accountability is grounded in memory rather than in surveillance, and that changes its tone. Nothing is described as being watched for; it is described as being retained. The asymmetry is the point: human beings lose the details of their own lives, which means the reckoning cannot be a matter of both sides comparing notes. Being informed of what one did is presented as the substance of the Day, before any sentence is mentioned.

crossReferences.why: Describes the record as a book that omits nothing, with people astonished at what it has kept.
Has hands and feet testify, which is the same idea of a record independent of the person's memory.
The long instruction to write debts down, showing how much apparatus human record-keeping needs.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things you did last Tuesday. Most people cannot manage it, and noticing that is the exercise. This ayah does not say your deeds are being judged harshly; it says they are being kept while you are losing them. Let that sit for a moment before you decide what today is worth.

studies.title: He Is Their Fourth
studies.meaning: Knowledge is stated in the widest possible terms and then immediately narrowed to a specific human scene. Three people lean together and He is the fourth; five, and He is the sixth. The numbers rise by twos, which is how private conversations actually grow, and the ayah then closes off every other size in a single clause. What began as an attribute has become a description of a room. Presence, not observation, is the word chosen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Private conferences were a live political problem in the town: groups meeting apart from the main body and letting others see that they were meeting. The commentators connect this ayah with the ayat that follow it about such gatherings, rather than reporting a separate occasion. Its argument is placed before the criticism, so the reasoning arrives ahead of the reproach it will support.

keyTerms.note: From a root for high ground set apart, then for drawing someone aside. The word is neutral in itself; it names talk held apart from others, which the surah goes on to sort by content rather than by secrecy.
An ordinal with a possessive ending, so it does not say a fourth is present but that He is theirs, counted into their group. The grammar puts Him inside the gathering rather than outside it.

The ordinary preposition for accompaniment. Classical commentators read it here as knowledge and encompassing rather than physical location, and note that the ayah opens and closes with knowing, which frames the word between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a settlement of clustered houses, courtyards and date gardens where sound carried. To speak apart from the crowd, people withdrew to the edge of a palm grove or lowered their voices in a corner of the mosque, and everyone could see them doing it. The visible fact of a huddle was itself information. A group counted from the outside is exactly three or five heads, which is why the ayah counts.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for confidential talk occurs in eleven ayat of the Quran, and five of them are in this one short surah, at 58:7, 58:8, 58:10, 58:12 and 58:13. No other surah uses it more than once. A chapter of twenty-two ayat thus holds nearly half the Quran's total use of the term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves from a general claim about knowledge to a claim about company, and the second is much harder to hold at arm's length. A person can accept that God knows everything and still feel alone in a room. Counting God into the gathering closes that gap by grammar rather than by argument. It also removes the idea of a private moral space, which is what secrecy assumes rather than what it achieves.

crossReferences.why: States the same nearness in the singular, closer than the jugular vein, where this ayah states it for a group.
Says God knows their confidential talk, using the same noun, in a passage about concealed intentions.
Answers those who suppose their secret talk is unheard, and adds that messengers are recording.

studies.applyIt: The next time you find yourself lowering your voice, pause on the reason. Some reasons are good ones: kindness, discretion, a confidence someone entrusted to you. Some are not. Ask yourself which this is before you carry on, and if the answer is the second kind, say the sentence at normal volume or not at all.

studies.title: The Greeting That Was Not
studies.meaning: The ayah tracks a pattern rather than a single act: a prohibition, a return to what was prohibited, and then a specific content given to the whispering. Sin, aggression and defiance of the messenger are named, so the objection is to what was being said, not to speaking privately. Then the scene shifts to the greeting at the door, courteous on the surface and altered underneath. The last move is inward, an argument they make silently to themselves from the absence of consequences.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators report that certain visitors twisted the customary greeting when they came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), altering a word so that it kept the sound of a blessing while carrying something else. Reports differ on who exactly, and the Quran does not name them. What is agreed is the setting: a period when hostility in Medina was expressed through etiquette and gossip rather than open confrontation.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root for life, because the Arabic greeting is a wish for long life or peace. Naming the act with that root sharpens the contrast: the form of the words wishes life while the intent does not.
From a root for crossing a limit and running past it. Set beside the word for sin, it separates wrongs that damage the doer from wrongs that reach across and land on someone else.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to become. It names where something ends up rather than where it is sent, so the word treats the destination as the result of a process.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greeting was the first test of a relationship in Arabia. How a traveller addressed a man on the road announced whether he came in peace, and a formula was expected within earshot of the household. Because the words were fixed, a small alteration was audible to anyone paying attention and deniable to anyone challenged on it. That is exactly the space a hostile guest could work in without ever being accused of an insult.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three-item list, sin and aggression and defiance of the messenger, appears twice in consecutive ayat, here and at 58:9, in identical wording. The first time it describes what a group was doing; the second time the identical phrase is addressed to believers as something to steer away from. The repetition is what converts a report into guidance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The delay of consequences is treated as an argument people actually make, and the Quran states it in their own voice before answering it. That is a serious concession: nothing in experience refutes the reasoning. The answer is not a demonstration but a horizon, which relocates the question from evidence to time. It also establishes that a courtesy performed with hostile intent is legible, so the outward form of speech is not where the account is settled.

crossReferences.why: Instructs that a greeting be returned with something better or its equal, the norm this passage shows being abused.
Describes the same gap between what is said outwardly and what is held inwardly.
Answers the same impatience for a punishment, noting that God is full of forgiveness despite people's wrongdoing.

studies.applyIt: Pick one greeting you say every day without meaning it, at the door, on a call, in a message. Say it once tomorrow while actually looking at the person and wanting for them what the words say. This ayah is about the distance between a formula and an intention. Closing that distance takes about three seconds.

studies.title: Change The Subject, Keep The Room
studies.meaning: Private conversation is left standing; it is redirected. The same three things named in the previous ayah are set out as what not to confer about, and then two positive words replace them: goodness and mindfulness of God. The structure keeps the practice and changes the content, which is a different move from banning the practice outright. The closing clause supplies the reason, naming the gathering to which all private gatherings eventually report.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to believers immediately after a description of others. The community in Medina was newly assembled from groups that had recently been at war with each other, and factions still met apart. An instruction that ruled out private talk altogether would have been unworkable in a town run by conversation. The commentators read this ayah as the constructive half of the passage, arriving once the problem has been described.

keyTerms.note: A wide word covering piety and practical decency together, used elsewhere of open land. It is not confined to ritual; the Quran defines it at length in one long passage as belief, spending, keeping promises and patience.

From a root for shielding oneself. It describes a protective alertness rather than dread, and pairing it with goodness gives the passage an inward and an outward term for the same redirected conversation.
A passive from a root for driving a crowd together into one place. It answers the private huddle with the largest possible assembly, and the passive leaves no one arranging their own attendance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Business in a caravan town was done in small groups: two partners settling a share, three men agreeing a price before the market opened, a family arranging a marriage. None of that could be conducted in the open without losing the deal. The instruction assumes people will keep meeting this way and asks only what passes between them, which is the difference between regulating a town and shutting it down.
studies.didYouKnow: Goodness and mindfulness of God appear as a pair elsewhere in the Quran, at 5:2, where people are told to help one another in exactly these two things. The same two words, in the same order, are given there as the alternative to cooperating in sin and aggression, which are also the words this ayah replaces.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Secrecy is not treated as a moral category on its own. What is weighed is content, which means privacy is neither a refuge nor a charge in itself, and the same act can go either way. That is a demanding position, because it removes the comfort of a rule that could be kept without judgement. The closing reference to a universal gathering supplies the only frame in which every private room is finally one room.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same two words for goodness and mindfulness against the same two words for sin and aggression.
Says there is no good in much of their private talk, except where it urges charity or reconciliation.
Addresses believers about suspicion and backbiting, the everyday form of the problem this ayah redirects.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group chat or a standing conversation with one friend where the register has slowly drifted towards other people's failings. You do not have to leave it. Introduce one different subject this week, something you actually want for someone. Notice whether the conversation follows you. This ayah keeps the meeting and changes what is on the table.

studies.title: Designed To Cause Grief
studies.meaning: The aim of the whispering is named, and it is not damage but grief. What the plotters were producing was a feeling in other people, the sense of being talked about and excluded. The ayah then separates that feeling from actual harm, which it says cannot occur except by permission. Nothing here denies the distress; it relocates it. The final clause is an instruction to redirect reliance, phrased so that the believers do it themselves rather than being reassured.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on private conferences. Believers in Medina could see groups meeting apart and could not hear what was said, and the commentators describe the resulting anxiety as the actual problem: people returning from the mosque uneasy about what had been discussed without them. No single occasion is reported. The ayah addresses the effect of the plotting rather than the plotters.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sorrow, not for injury. Naming grief as the objective identifies the tactic precisely: the plotting worked by being visible, and what it produced in onlookers was its whole purpose.
An active participle under a negation, which denies the capacity rather than a particular act. The construction says the adversary is not a harmer of them at all, before the exception is stated.

A command in the third person, from a root for appointing someone to act on one's behalf. Reliance here is delegation of an outcome, not passivity, and the form leaves the doing to the believers themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a town of a few thousand, exclusion was a weapon that cost nothing. A man who saw three others fall silent as he approached had no way to find out what had been said, and no way to ask without appearing suspicious. Reputation moved by talk, and talk moved fastest in the gaps between people. Anxiety about being discussed was not vanity there; it was a reasonable calculation about one's safety.
studies.didYouKnow: The command to rely on God in this third-person form, which leaves the believers as the ones who act, occurs nine times in the Quran and clusters at moments of pressure rather than of ease. It closes a passage on battle at 3:160 and appears in the mouths of prophets under threat at 12:67 and 14:12. Here it answers a purely social injury.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Causation is placed under permission without denying that people plot. The adversary is granted a strategy and refused an outcome, which keeps human malice real while removing its final authority. This matters for how fear is handled: the passage does not tell believers that nobody is against them, and it does not promise that nothing will happen. It moves the question of what can actually reach them to a different desk.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the same third-person command to rely, after stating that no one can help if God withholds.
Calls the adversary's scheming weak, which is the same downgrading of an opponent's apparent power.
Jacob takes precautions and then says the decision belongs to God alone, holding both together.

studies.applyIt: Think of a room you were not in this week, a decision made without you, a message you were left off. Name what you actually lost, in plain words, and then name what you only felt. Usually the second list is longer. This ayah separates those two things before it asks anything of you.

studies.title: Make Room, Be Raised
studies.meaning: Two small instructions about a crowded room, and a promise attached to each. Make space when asked, and space will be made for you. Stand up and move when asked, and the response is a raising in rank. Scholars differ over whether the two groups at the end are one, believers who have knowledge, or two, believers and then scholars among them. Either way, rank is attached to something other than the seat you got.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this ayah to the crowding around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the mosque, where people arriving late found no room and those already seated were reluctant to move. Reports vary in their details, including which group was involved, but they agree on the setting: a small space, a growing community, and the ordinary friction of who sits where.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning wide and open. The reply promises the same verb back from God, without saying in what, so the room made for you is left unspecified and the commentators list many kinds.
A verb of getting up from a seat and of raised ground. Classical readers take it as standing to make space, or as leaving when the gathering ends, and both are recorded without a decision.
The word for the rungs of a ladder or the tiers of a building, left indefinite and plural here. What is promised is not a position but a distance travelled upward, and no number is given.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seating was status. In an Arab gathering the place nearest the leader was contested, and where a man sat told everyone what he was worth that year. The mosque in Medina was a courtyard with a roof of palm branches over part of it, and it filled. Latecomers stood at the back. An instruction to give up a good seat cost something real, which is why it needed an ayah.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 58 is the only chapter of the Quran in which the divine name occurs in every single one of its twenty-two ayat, without exception. It is also named after a woman who argued her case with the Prophet, and the surah opens by saying God heard the dispute, which is the reason the whole chapter keeps that name in view.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A rule of etiquette is given a theological return. Making physical space is answered with space from God, in the same word, so a courtesy is treated as an act with consequences beyond the room. The second half then reorders a gathering by an invisible standard. Belief and knowledge are named as what raises a person, which leaves the seating arrangement in the room disconnected from the ranking that matters.

crossReferences.why: Asks the question this ayah answers, placing those who know on a different footing from those who do not.
Gives the only request for increase the Prophet is instructed to make, and it is for knowledge.
Reorders a gathering by a different invisible measure, replacing lineage with awareness of God.

studies.applyIt: In the next meeting or gathering you attend, move over before anyone asks. Give the better seat, the closer spot, the place with the view. Nobody will notice, which is part of it. The ayah attaches a promise to the small physical act rather than to the feeling behind it, so the act is the whole assignment.
